paragraphs: If the whole is to be set in order and the commonwealth put into the best possible shape, several relations must be considered. First, there is the action of the whole body upon itself, the relation of the whole to the whole, of the Sovereign to the State; and this relation, as we shall see, is made up of the relations of the intermediate terms.

The laws that regulate this relation are called political laws, and also fundamental laws, not without reason if they are wise. For if each State has only one good system, the people that possesses it should hold fast to it; but if the established order is bad, why should laws that prevent men from being good be regarded as fundamental? Besides, in any case a people is always in a position to change its laws, however good; for if it chooses to do itself harm, who can have a right to stop it?

The second relation is that of the members to one another, or to the body as a whole; and this relation should be as unimportant as possible in the first respect and as important as possible in the second. Each citizen would then be perfectly independent of all the others, and at the same time very dependent on the city; and this is always brought about by the same means, since only the strength of the State can secure the liberty of its members. From this second relation arise civil laws.

We may also consider a third kind of relation, between the individual and the law: the relation of disobedience to its penalty. This gives rise to the establishment of criminal laws, which are, at bottom, less a particular class of law than the sanction behind all the rest.

Along with these three kinds of law goes a fourth, the most important of all, which is not engraved on tablets of marble or brass but on the hearts of the citizens. This forms the real constitution of the State; it takes on new strength every day; when other laws decay or die out, it revives them or takes their place; it keeps a people in the ways it was meant to follow, and insensibly replaces authority with the force of habit. I am speaking of morals, of custom, above all of public opinion: a power unknown to political thinkers, on which nonetheless success in everything else depends. With this the great legislator concerns himself in secret, though he seems to confine himself to particular regulations; for these are only the arc of the arch, while manners and morals, slower to arise, form in the end its immovable keystone.
Among the different classes of laws, only the political laws, which determine the form of the government, are relevant to my subject.
